title: All the key moments from the 2026 Bahrain GP in Malaysia
excerpt:
The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia delivered an action-packed weekend, culminating in Max Verstappen reaching the top step of the podium for the first time in 2026.

There were also plenty of other talking points that emerged across the three days of action, from George Russell’s dramatic retirement to the Sepang International Circuit staging a thriller on its return to F1.

Here are all the key moments from the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia…

Verstappen and Red Bull get back to winning ways

Red Bull took on a huge challenge in the build-up to F1’s all-new 2026 regulations by investing in their own power unit facility and creating an engine from the ground up.

With that in mind, Verstappen and team mate Isack Hadjar’s combined tally of nine Grand Prix podium finishes across the first 15 rounds of the season was rather impressive – plenty of promise being shown, even if reliability caused a few headaches.

Verstappen and Red Bull are winners, though, and podiums were not going to satisfy them for much longer.

After coming within two tenths of victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, the Dutchman and his team continued their positive momentum into the Sepang weekend, where Verstappen triumphed on F1’s last visit to the Malaysian venue back in 2017.

Using plenty of lessons from the first half of the season, and boosted by recent updates, Verstappen charged to a breakthrough 2026 pole position on Saturday – lapping almost three tenths quicker than nearest challenger Lewis Hamilton.

While Sunday threw everything at the drivers, including heavy rain, suspended starts, delays, mixed conditions, Safety Car restarts and more, nothing could stop the four-time World Champion from converting that pole into the race win.

It might have come too late for a championship comeback this year, but underlines that Verstappen and Red Bull are a force to be reckoned with once more, and should head into 2027 as serious contenders.

Verstappen 'incredibly proud' after historic Bahrain GP win

Mixed fortunes for Mercedes as the title battle takes a big turn

There were contrasting fortunes for the two Mercedes drivers in Sepang. Kimi Antonelli grabbed a podium to extend his lead in the championship, and while it was not the win, second place on a day where treacherous conditions could have derailed his title charge was a very strong result, but one that the team would likely describe as bittersweet.

That is because George Russell failed to finish, his power unit giving up the ghost with only a handful of laps to go. Prior to this the Briton had struggled to match his team mate in Malaysia, despite getting past Antonelli early on.

He could not hold the Italian at bay once Antonelli got his tyres up to temperature, and was unable to stick with the youngster despite him at one point running wide and collecting a bollard.

But Russell was on for a solid P3 and thus would have only lost a further three points to Antonelli in the title fight. His DNF means the gap between the two now stands at 84 points, or over three Grand Prix victories.

Russell’s DNF was not the only disappointment for the team, with the first big upgrade package bolted onto the car since Canada not having the desired effect. Mercedes struggled for pace with respect to Red Bull across the weekend as a whole, and could not get that set-up into the sweet spot.

They have work to do to understand those updates before Singapore next weekend, but in Antonelli they do have a driver in fine form, who was able to put his mistakes from Baku firmly behind him and deliver the sort of performance that has taken him to such a commanding lead in the standings.

Superb recovery drives as Ferrari fail to nail strategy calls

Ferrari were not the only team caught out by the track conditions, but their decision to fit both cars with soft tyres when the race got underway nearly proved their undoing. On a wet track, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc plummeted down the order, the latter’s day made worse with contact that forced an early pit stop.

Hamilton deserves credit for holding his nerve, staying out on the softs as others realised their mistake and pitted for intermediates, and getting the C4 rubber to work for him as conditions began to dry.

He climbed back up the order with a drive reminiscent of some of his very best from days gone by, and would likely have challenged for third even without the late Safety Car bunching up the field.

The seven-time World Champion recorded his first rostrum since Silverstone with that P3 finish, leading many to wonder what might have been had he started on the intermediates like the Red Bull and Mercedes drivers.

As for Leclerc, his recovery took longer after he found himself last thanks to that contact and subsequent pit stop. But he deserves equal credit for working hard to climb back into the top 10, a late move on Isack Hadjar bagging him P4 – the position he believes he would have finished in no matter what.

Leclerc relieved with P4 after everything went 'wrong' in Sepang

A hectic afternoon for McLaren

For McLaren it was an eventful race too, with both cars being amongst a small number to start on the slick medium tyres in still-wet conditions.

After initially falling back, Oscar Piastri pitted for intermediates at the end of the first lap while Lando Norris stayed out – something the Briton said after the race was a “gamble”.

When the track dried out, both drivers moved through the field, with the Australian winding up ahead of his team mate despite making an extra stop and not running on the clearly favoured soft tyre at any point.

There was a hairy moment for the McLaren pit wall when Norris nearly crashed into the back of Piastri as the cars ahead bunched up following George Russell’s retirement under the late Safety Car, with Norris running off track and dropping down the order as a result.

The reigning World Champion ultimately recovered to finish P9 – and later received a reprimand for driving erratically under Safety Car conditions – with Piastri taking the chequered flag in sixth place.

Alonso secures points for Aston Martin

Despite Fernando Alonso’s record of winning three times with three different teams in Sepang, before this weekend it seemed a long shot that he could bring his Aston Martin home in the points after the squad’s beleaguered season so far.

But the Spaniard did just that, finishing in eighth place, while team mate Lance Stroll was not far behind either in P12.

The AMR26 suddenly showed signs of promise when it hit the track in Malaysia, with both drivers getting into Q2 on merit and gaining a few grid places thanks to penalties around them.

Alonso started on medium tyres for Sunday’s race and dropped back, before pitting for the hard compound and running a long stint.

He managed to stay out of trouble, benefitted from other incidents, and had fresh softs for the end to fight with - holding on to deny Lando Norris by half a second to finish P8, his best result of the season, and bringing back some much-needed points for the Silverstone-based outfit.

While Stroll couldn’t quite match Alonso’s result, the Canadian later said that he had enjoyed being able to battle in the race and fight towards the points – something the Aston Martin drivers have not been able to say for some time.

Sepang delivers a thriller on its F1 return

As touched on earlier, F1 had not raced at Sepang for almost a decade when Malaysia agreed to step in and stage the Bahrain Grand Prix.

For the drivers who had previously experienced the venue, it was a welcome return, and for those who had not, there were plenty of smiles during Friday practice as they got to grips with a fast and flowing layout.

The hot, humid conditions understandably posed a challenge, as did the tyre degradation seen throughout FP1, FP2 and FP3 – leading to the prospect of a fascinating, strategic Grand Prix on Sunday.

The situation was flipped on its head when the heavens opened around an hour before the race start, though, soaking the track and setting up a race that started in damp conditions and transitioned to the dry.

On a chaotic afternoon, there was action from start to finish to keep the many thousands of passionate fans watching trackside on the edge of their seats, as Sepang delivered another F1 classic that will be remembered for years to come.

title: Wolff ‘not in a happy place’ after Russell Malaysia DNF
excerpt:
Toto Wolff admitted that he was “not in a happy place” after George Russell suffered a late retirement from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia due to a power unit issue, with the Mercedes boss stating that the race had been “one of my worst experiences”.

After bringing upgrades to Sepang, the Silver Arrows were hopeful for their prospects. However, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen outpaced them to secure pole position before converting this into his first win of the season.

Kimi Antonelli managed to hold onto second place in what proved to be an eventful afternoon with changing weather conditions, but Russell’s day ended in disaster when he was forced to pull off to the side of the track just a few laps from the finish.

With it marking the Briton’s third retirement of the season – and the team’s fourth, Antonelli having suffered a mechanical failure in Barcelona – Wolff was left feeling frustrated by how the team’s race had panned out.

“It's a PU failure,” he explained of Russell’s DNF to Sky Sports F1. “It wasn't caused by the Safety Car, so we haven't assessed it yet.

“I'm so massively annoyed and not in a happy place. First of all, we didn't have the speed that we were hoping to have before the weekend, so there's a lot of homework to be done in order to recover, which I'm sure we will.

“Then the race literally, if you consider the fight with Lewis [Hamilton] behind, went against us. We had such an advantage, [but then] two VSCs or one VSC, two Safety Cars… you couldn't be more unlucky.

“To make things worse, a PU failure with a few laps to go to the end with George, which is terrible for his championship and not good at all for our constructor points. So as much as I love to be here, when I look at the pure race, it's one of my worst experiences, to be honest."

While Wolff took heart from Antonelli’s result, the Austrian remained unhappy about the potential impact that further retirements could have for Mercedes.

“[Kimi] scored a few more points than Lewis behind him,” said Wolff. “I'm happy because he did the job. But it's just this overarching topic, the DNFs, that could cost us dearly also for the remaining seven races.

“A championship is quickly turned around against you, if you have a DNF, and that's why that can't continue.”

Despite this, Wolff admitted that he is taking positives from his belief in the team’s ability to turn things around.

“I think we have a good action plan,” the Team Principal continued. “James [Allison, Technical Director] is really fully on top of it with his leadership team. That lifts my mood, because I know we have such a tremendous group of people, and the same way as with HPP [High Performance Powertrains], they're going to sort it out.

“But that gives me real relief for the moment to know they are the best, and they are going to find a solution, and I think that we will come back strong.”

title: How Hadjar lost a possible podium chance in Sepang
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar always sets high standards for himself, and the Red Bull driver is rarely completely satisfied with a race result.

Perhaps not surprisingly then, Hadjar was left bitterly disappointed after a potential podium finish slipped out of his hands due to a battery issue for his Red Bull machine in the closing laps of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Instead he fell back to finish P5 – still good progress from his penalised P8 starting position, but far less than he had anticipated at one point in the race.

Having made the optimum choice for intermediate tyres at the start he immediately moved up, taking advantage of the fact that four cars ahead started on slicks, while also losing one spot to Liam Lawson.

By Lap 6 he had passed the man who kept his RB22 seat warm for three races to claim fourth, and from there he initially had a good view of the battle up ahead that featured his team mate Max Verstappen and Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

However any hopes he may have had of joining the fight faded as he struggled for grip and couldn’t match the pace of the guys ahead – and he had no explanation as to why.

“No, but something was wrong,” Hadjar said. “Because I can't possibly be a second lap slower now, even compared to a Mercedes, where the whole weekend we were quicker. And now in the race we're absolutely nowhere. The car was horrible to drive.”

The Frenchman's struggles were evident in his surprised response on the radio when later in the race he was told that he was fighting Lewis Hamilton – who at one stage was far behind in his Ferrari.

"Yeah, he was 15 seconds behind me, and then in a couple of laps he was [right] behind, when the whole weekend I was pretty fast. Yeah, we need to fix the issue, and come back in Singapore and do better.”

Hadjar was still fourth during the last Safety Car period, and he then gained a spot when Russell stopped on track. However after the restart he struggled with a battery issue, and in the closing laps he was passed by first Hamilton, and then Charles Leclerc.

“Just the last couple of laps, I don't know how we ended up having no battery,” he said. “So in the straight, I couldn't defend against the Ferraris, so we lost the podium on something so stupid.

“I think the power unit was fine. It's just the first two laps of the restart, I don't know why we were so down on battery. Then it stabilised itself, and then I was fast again. Otherwise, I would have kept third.”

However, the main issue was chassis-related: “I don't know, just the grip – even behind the Safety Car, I was feeling that I had no grip, and it was going to be a tough restart for me. So it felt like I was always on the same tyres – I came back on the run one compound – so it's a joke.”

It was a great day for Verstappen, the Red Bull team and Ford as they logged the first win of the 2026 season, but Hadjar was in no mood to celebrate: “It's not a good day for me. I'm happy for the boys – but yeah, it's a disaster for me…”

title: Leclerc relieved with P4 after everything went ‘wrong’ in Sepang
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc conceded "everything that could have gone wrong...did go wrong" after dropping to last in the early stages of his race in Sepang, before he recovered to finish fourth.

Like his team mate Lewis Hamilton, the Monegasque managed to make his way back through the field to finish solidly in the points for Ferrari, despite a chaotic race that included contact, a strategy error and even a puncture.

Ferrari initially made the wrong call when the race finally got underway in wet-dry conditions, opting to put both drivers on the soft compound tyre. The track was still too wet, and as both fell back down the order, overtaken by those fitted with intermediates, Leclerc was called in to pit.

That was not just to get rid of his slicks – contact with Nico Hulkenberg had left him with a puncture and front wing damage. A slow pit stop to change his front wing and swap to the intermediates saw the Monegasque driver emerge in last position.

“I’m not sure how much more we could have done in terms of position with a completely smooth race to be honest," Leclerc explained.

"Everything that could have gone wrong in the first half of the race did go wrong, everything that could have gone right though in the second part of the race went right for us.

“At the end of the day, I think P4 on my side was the best I could do. I didn’t have a good feeling with the car, had quite a lot of inconsistencies and just struggled to use the maximum potential of the car and then obviously the first part of the race was very, very tricky with the slick tyres first, and then with the puncture and the broken front wing.

“And then just trying to save what we could save, and P4 at the end of the day is a good result considering the first part of the race.”

Hamilton dropped to 17th after starting on the softs, but managed to score an unlikely podium, meaning Ferrari extended their advantage over McLaren in the Constructors’ Championship, and marginally closed the gap to Mercedes.

The twin recovery drives showed the Ferrari had decent race pace in the mixed conditions, although the strategy calls made the Grand Prix more difficult than it could have been.

However, at a weekend where there was plenty of off-track noise regarding the future of Team Principal Fred Vasseur to filter out, Leclerc was proud of his result – but admitted the team need to learn from their mistakes.

“Relatively happy that we have done I think the best we could do at a weekend like this. But if we look back at the race, I think it is one of those races where the end result is maybe the maximum we could have done.

“But as a team there are plenty of things we need to learn from and do better next time we find ourselves in these conditions. But anyway, I’m happy we have a good race here and hopefully that stops a little bit the silly rumours that there are on the team.

“Fred is doing absolutely everything in order to bring back the team to the top, and we are all doing that, and to see all of these headlines in the last few days haven’t been nice at all.

“We are very united, that is the most important and I just hope we are back on the top step of the podium as soon as possible.”

title: What the teams said – Race day in Malaysia
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit.

Oct 04, 2026 2:11pm UTC

Red Bull

Max Verstappen took his first win of the season, but he did have to work a little more than planned to take the victory. On the inters, he was picked off by both Mercedes cars at the initial standing start, and even came under pressure from Lawson. But when the first Safety Car came out, Red Bull made the right call to put the Dutchman onto the softs.

On those, he was able to easily get Russell and then Antonelli at the restart, and from there he disappeared up the road. The pack concertinaed up thanks to a second Safety Car, but with more soft tyres onboard, Verstappen was able to hold Antonelli at bay to take a deserved win.

As for Isack Hadjar, he drove a lonely race in fourth, until Hamilton joined him. From there he put in a strong defensive drive to keep the Ferrari man at bay, but struggled with understeer at the final Safety Car restart and lost out to both Hamilton and Leclerc, and nearly Piastri too.

Max Verstappen, 1st

“What an incredible result! The race was not made easy for us with all the decisions we had to make and then the Safety Car at the end on top of everything. But we made all the right calls with the tyres, kept our cool, and it all paid off. Of course, to win a race in the first year of being a new power unit manufacturer is honestly just incredible and something everyone should be really proud of. We knew from the start that Red Bull Ford Powertrains built a strong engine and also knew the limitations too. Although it was hard at times, and we sometimes didn’t believe we could get this win, we kept pushing. The Team has also been working hard to understand our issues and brought performance upgrades to the car. Step by step, we have been getting closer and today we did it, which is really special and an emotional moment. It is an incredible project and winning in our first season together is a fantastic feeling."

Isack Hadjar, 5th

“Even though we managed to score P5, I am obviously frustrated. The car didn't feel as good as it did on the previous days, and then I didn't have the power after the restart at the end for two laps. If this hadn't have happened, I am sure I would have been on the podium. Despite this, it was a good overall result for the Team. I can't wait to look at the data and see what happened, then regroup and go again in Singapore. It is a track that I really, really like, so I will of course be pushing for the best result possible there."

Laurent Mekies, Team Principal

"This is another milestone moment in the history of this Team: the first victory for us as a power unit manufacturer with Red Bull Ford Powertrains in its very first season! The credit goes to all the people involved who have been working incredibly hard on this project over the past five years. Everyone in Milton Keynes and at the track deserves this moment and should celebrate it as an important step towards many more victories in the future.

"The first win of the season is a great way to finish what has been an extremely successful weekend overall. After showing strong pace in every session and securing our first pole position of the season yesterday, Max converted that performance into an outstanding P1 today. In often chaotic circumstances, he remained in control throughout the race, managed the conditions brilliantly, showed the strongest pace and delivered exactly the kind of performance we know he is capable of.

"More broadly, this result confirms the progress we have been making in recent months. We were already close several times, and today we converted that pace. The Team has been working tirelessly to improve our package, and weekends like this are the reward for that effort.

"There are naturally mixed feelings on the other side of the garage because Isack also showed very strong pace all weekend. We could have rounded off this weekend with another double podium; unfortunately, not everything went well with his car. Finishing fifth still represents a strong result considering where he started, but naturally it is frustrating when you know more was possible. We will analyse exactly what happened, take the positives from a weekend where both drivers were consistently competitive, and immediately turn our focus to Singapore.

"For tonight, however, everyone should enjoy a well-deserved victory and an important milestone for this Team."

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Race winner Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing celebrates on the podium during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains leads Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Mercedes

Mercedes made the right call to start both cars on the inters, with Kimi Antonelli charging off the line into the lead and George Russell following him through into second. But when they fitted the mediums under the first Safety Car, that left the duo at the mercy of the soft-shod Verstappen. Once he went past both, Russell briefly got his team mate but Antonelli fought his way back in front and from there the Italian was the faster of the duo.

They looked on for a straightforward double podium, until Russell suffered late heartbreak as he pulled off with an apparent PU failure. Head in hands, Russell’s title chances lay in tatters as Antonelli went to score 18 points and extend his lead in the Drivers’ Championship to 84 points.

Kimi Antonelli, 2nd

"Overall, given our struggles this weekend, I think P2 was the maximum we could have achieved today. The conditions were really challenging, both with the difficult call on which tyre to start on, when to stop to take the slicks, and then when to stop and what compound to take to ensure we held on to second. The team did a good job with those calls, and I am pleased we were able to score solid points.

"Despite that, we leave Malaysia frustrated. Our pace hasn’t been where we wanted it to be and we weren’t able to fight for victory. It was also extremely disappointing to see George retire when we were so close to such a good result for the team, and a double podium at what is one of the most significant races in our season. We will work hard ahead of Singapore to understand how we can improve and make sure we perform more strongly next weekend."

George Russell, DNF

"That was another tough and disappointing day for me amongst several we have had this season. It is pure bad luck, but it still hurts. It is particularly tough as we were on for a podium and a great result for the team. I made a great start on the Intermediate but struggled a little once we moved to the Medium tyre. I felt much better once we were on the Soft compound and, whilst we were never in the fight for the win, our pace was good.

"It’s such a shame to retire from the race when we were looking comfortable in P3. It would have been important points in the Constructors’ for the team and a double podium would have been a lovely reward for our Title and Technical Partner PETRONAS as their home race.

"It’s not been an easy weekend, but our race pace was better than our qualifying performance on Saturday. That is encouraging but we will work hard as a team to understand why we have underperformed overall here in Malaysia and how we can make sure we are stronger in Singapore. It has been a tough season on my side of the garage, but we will keep fighting."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"This has been our worst weekend of the season. It hurts, and I feel incredibly sorry for George and everyone in the team. George drove an outstanding race and was on course for a very strong result, but we let him down. The reality is that has happened too often this year, and that is not acceptable.

"We were not quick enough, and we were not reliable enough in Malaysia. That is the truth. Both drivers kept fighting, stayed focused, and got everything out of the car that was possible though. Whilst George lost out through no fault of his own, Kimi did a very good job and deserved his podium.

"Now we need to understand exactly what happened this weekend. We underperformed compared to our nearest competitors and our form in recent races. We will do so with our usual focus, by working diligently and being led by the data. We don't have many days before we are on track again, but we are determined to put on a better showing next week in Singapore."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"Today was a difficult race to manage, particularly in the opening stages when we had to make several important decisions around tyre choice and crossover points as the conditions evolved. The team made good calls throughout the afternoon and we were able to maximise Kimi's race, bringing home a well-deserved podium. He drove a mature and controlled race and extracted everything that was available to him.

"For George, it's incredibly frustrating. He was driving a strong race, managing the conditions well, and looked on course for a comfortable podium before his retirement. Losing a result like that at any race is painful, but especially when he has suffered so much bad luck so far this season.

"Whilst there are positives we can take from today's race execution, we weren’t quick enough to fight for the win. We have a lot of data to review and very little time before we are back on track in Singapore. Our focus now is on understanding the factors that have contributed to this weekend's performance and identifying where we can improve. Singapore presents a very different challenge, and our job over the next few days is to make sure we arrive there better prepared and in a position to be more competitive."

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Second placed Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team lifts his trophy on the podium during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: George Russell of Great Britain and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team is given a ride by a marshal after retiring from the race during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains overtakes Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Ferrari had a very up and down day in Sepang to say the least. Starting both cars on slicks, they plummeted down the order on a still wet track, with Charles Leclerc called in for inters, dropping to last place via some contact with Hulkenberg’s Audi. Lewis Hamilton opted to “gamble” in his own words and stayed out on the softs. He was a minute off the lead, but got that soft compound working and started to climb back through the field and even into the points.

He steadily made his way forward until he found himself right behind Hadjar in a fight for fourth. A Safety Car enabled both to stop and Hamilton was put on the unfancied mediums. But he was able to swap back to the softs under the late Safety Car, and on those was able to pick off the Red Bull for what had seemed an unlikely podium. Leclerc recovered to fourth, also making his way past Hadjar late on.

Lewis Hamilton, 3rd

"Sepang is always a great track to race on, but today is definitely one of the most memorable. It was a really demanding race and not an easy one to manage from the start, but the team did a fantastic job staying calm and executing well after a difficult opening phase. We found ourselves on the back foot very early on with the tyre choice, yet everyone stayed focused and kept pushing. We didn't give up despite a big gap building straight away, and step by step we managed to fight our way back into contention and keep the pressure on until the flag.

"To finish on the podium after the way the race began feels really satisfying and is a great reward for the hard work, determination and resilience everyone showed today. A big thank you as well to the fans, who were incredible all weekend."

Charles Leclerc, 4th

"It was an eventful race. A lot of things went wrong in the first part, and everything that could have gone right did in the second part, so I would say P4 is a good result today all things considered.

"I collided with Nico [Hulkenberg] on lap 1 as I started on slicks and the track turned out to still be very wet. It was a close call which tyres to start on, with a mixed grid, and we will learn from today to be prepared should these conditions come up again.

"We’re heading to Singapore next, so let’s see what we can bring home for the team there."

Fred Vasseur, Team Principal

"Overall our result is good, especially considering where we were at the end of the first lap. To finish third and fourth after dropping to the back of the field is a very strong comeback from the whole team.

"The tyre choice on the grid was a difficult one: in those conditions, you can only judge from what you see around you on the grid and in the pit lane. We did not have the full picture of the track and, in the end, we got the call wrong. We will analyse everything carefully and make sure we learn from it for the future.

"From that moment on, we stayed calm, executed well and made the right decisions. The strategy worked as intended, our pace was strong and both Lewis and Charles did an excellent job managing their tyres while fighting their way back through the field. Charles' race was made even more difficult by the need to stop after the first lap to replace the front wing following a collision, which makes his recovery to fourth place particularly impressive.

"We scored good points, secured another podium and showed strong pace in difficult conditions."

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Charles Leclerc of Monaco and Scuderia Ferrari walks underneath an umbrella as he shelters from the rain on the grid prior to the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

Like Ferrari, McLaren gambled on the slicks at the start. With both cars on the mediums, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri lost out to most of the intermediate runners with the Australian coming in to swap to the green-marked tyre. That proved the right call, as he climbed forward while Norris could not get his mediums to work.

Both pitted for hards under the first Safety Car and slowly recovered, but they could not stick with the soft-shod Hamilton who was also scything his way back through the field. The next pit stop saw Norris put on softs, the best race tyre and he climbed back behind his team mate, who had fitted a second set of hards.

But there was more drama to come, Norris nearly hitting his team mate as he was caught out by the pack closing up behind the last Safety Car. He ran wide into the gravel, dropping out of the top 10. The last few racing laps saw Norris recover again into the points, while Piastri ran out of time to pick off Hadjar.

Lando Norris, 9th

"Ultimately, today boiled down to a few key issues. The initial gamble to start on the medium tyres didn't work out; the grip just wasn't there as we had anticipated, it was a collective decision, and in hindsight, it was the wrong one. However, we also simply weren't quick enough, and we have to be honest about that. The car is lacking pace, and we need to improve it significantly if we want to be competitive. I don't think we could fight for more than P6 and P7 today, regardless of how we executed the race.

"The incident behind the Safety Car was my mistake. The pack ahead checked up much more suddenly because of the situation with George, and I just got caught out. It was a very unusual and unlucky situation, but at the end of the day, it's my responsibility to manage that. I know I could have done better today, just as the team knows we have work to do in making the car quicker. We will learn from today and turn our focus to preparing for Singapore."

Oscar Piastri, 6th

“P6. It was a very mixed and chaotic race today. We took a gamble at the start with the slick tyres, and then immediately boxed for Inters, but the change was the right call, and the Safety Car timing allowed us to minimise the effect of it. We improved a lot on the Hard tyres, especially in the second stint where we were catching Leclerc, which the final Safety Car cut short. However, we just didn’t have the pace we needed today to make a lasting impact.

“We know the work we have to do and that we need to keep pushing and bringing further developments to the car to close that gap - we can see the progress our rivals are making, which was clear from Red Bull’s performance this weekend. Our new parts are performing as expected, but everyone else is also improving, so we are not currently in the fight for wins. We’ll review it all and then focus on Singapore.”

Andrea Stella, Team Principal

“It was a race packed with incidents, just as we’d expected. Setting aside any assessment of the decisions made at crucial moments – the tyres at the start, the timing of the pit stops – the reality is that this weekend our car package was fourth in terms of performance. Even if we’d got every decision spot on, I don’t think we could have achieved any higher than Oscar’s sixth place. Of course, we could have picked up a few more points with Lando had it not been for his excursion onto the run-off area at the second restart, but in terms of assessing our overall performance, it wouldn’t have made a difference.

“We need to analyse the results of the last two races carefully and work out how to get our performance back to the level we saw around the summer break, when we secured two wins and three Pole positions. Certainly, some of our direct rivals have taken a significant step forward – such as Red Bull – and now it’s up to us to respond so that we can get back into the fight for podium places and try to improve our position in both championships.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes leads Alexander Albon of Thailand driving the (23) Williams FW48 Mercedes and Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sam Bagnall/Sutton Images)

Racing Bulls

Both Racing Bulls cars made brilliant starts on the inters, Liam Lawson vying with Verstappen for third while Arvid Lindblad found himself in the top 10 from the final row of the grid. Both fitted hard tyres under the first Safety Car, and that left them a little vulnerable. Lawson was sensible, not fighting the out-of-position front runners when they made their way back through the field. On the hard tyre, the Kiwi racer might have found things tricky had there not been so much drama behind him.

Fortunately, the team had some softs to fit for the final stint, and he was able to come home ‘best of the rest’. Lindblad was involved in much of that drama, racing wheel-to-wheel with the likes of Ocon, Bortoleto and Hulkenberg. He initially looked set to miss out on points after falling to P11, but he picked off the Audi on the very last lap to make it a very strong day for the team.

Arvid Lindblad, 10th

"Today was definitely action packed with all the pit stops and Safety Cars. We finished with an amazing result and the team did a really good job making all the right calls at the right moments, so massive credit to everyone. Even though I feel like I could have done a bit more on my side, there are definitely a lot of positives to take from today, especially as it was my first time driving in the wet. We’re now moving on to the final leg of the triple-header, and with Singapore being a Sprint weekend, I’m hoping we can pick up some more points and have another interesting race.”

Liam Lawson, 7th

"It feels great to be taking home double points from the Bahrain GP in Malaysia, as we continue to fight for P5 in the Championship. I had one of the best starts of my life today and then we managed to maintain a strong position at the front of the midfield for the duration of the race. Our car has been very good all weekend and the strategy throughout the race was on point. Seeing our Power Unit take home the victory also rounds off a solid effort from the team both back at the factory and trackside, so a huge thanks to everyone. We'll be taking all the positives and learnings from this weekend as we head to Singapore tonight. It's a Sprint weekend for the first time there too, so I'm looking forward to maximising all the point scoring opportunities."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"It felt like a long race today, but it also went by in a flash. It’s been great to be back here in Malaysia; standing on the grid in the pouring rain this afternoon felt like we’d never been away. This place always gives us a spicy race and that’s certainly what we got.

“We definitely got the basics right today; the choice for Inter tyres was the correct one especially as the cars went out, you could see there was huge spray. For Liam it was quite a straightforward race, there were no threats from behind and we stopped under the Safety Car for the first set of Hard tyres and then stopped for the second set later on in the race. Arvid had a little bit of a tougher day, he suffered with a lot more tyre degradation than Liam did, but he’s had good pace all weekend and did a great job getting past Nico [Hulkenberg] on that final lap, bringing home that extra point. Whilst we come away with some impressive points today, it’s far from over, so we’ll take all our learnings into Singapore to finish the triple header.

“A huge well done to everyone at track and back at home in Faenza and a huge congratulations to everyone at Red Bull Ford Powertrains – a first win in its first season – very impressive, congratulations!”

(Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford and Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes battle for track position during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

Aston Martin

Aston Martin managed to score for just the second time this season, despite starting the race on the slick tyres. Both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll fell backwards on the mediums, and while the Canadian pitted for inters, Alonso hung it out with the likes of Hamilton and Norris.

Somehow, the Spaniard was able to extract decent pace not just from his car, but from two sets of the unfancied hard tyre. Bolting on some new softs under the Safety Car, Alonso muscled his way into the points and even had the pace to hold Norris at bay on the last lap. Stroll came close to his best race of the season, running out of time to fight for the top 10.

Fernando Alonso, 8th

“We have been more competitive this weekend and P8 is a good result for us. There were a lot of things that happened in the race. We started with the dry tyres and put ourselves in a difficult position, but thankfully the Safety Car started a new race for us. There are not many weekends where we can score points, so we executed well and took the opportunity. Let’s see if we can keep up this pace into Singapore where on paper we have some hope. The issues at the start were quite strange and we need to understand what happened there.”

Lance Stroll, 12th

“We came to Malaysia knowing this track would suit our car slightly better – less power and grip limited so that helped us. It was fun being out there today and battling with other cars. The weather conditions were very tricky and I think we missed some good racing with the delayed start. But I was surprised how slippery it was when I first got out there so I came in and switched to Inters, which was the right choice. The Hard tyre seemed very robust and I think I could have pushed the second set we used more in hindsight. That’s where we lost a couple of positions and finished outside the points.”

Mike Krack, Chief Trackside Officer

“It’s great to score four points and achieve our best result of the year, with Fernando in P8 and Lance in P12. Both drivers were in the mix throughout the afternoon, executing some strong overtakes and making the most of the opportunities that came their way. It’s encouraging to convert the speed we showed in qualifying into race results. So much happened this afternoon, from the rainy conditions to the delayed start, so we need to conduct a thorough review of how things played out and some of the decisions we made. It’s also important that we thank Bahrain and Malaysia for their fantastic collaboration in making this race possible with just a couple of months’ notice.”

(Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Lance Stroll of Canada driving the (18) Aston Martin F1 Team AMR26 Honda on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Audi

Audi might wonder how they did not manage to score in Sepang. They started on the softs with both cars, but made the call to quickly pit both for inters. As such, their cars were able to negate some of that time lost and start to climb forward. But Bortoleto’s day was undone fighting with Sainz, the Brazilian trying a move down the inside of Turn 2. He clipped the Williams, the stewards finding him at fault and handing Gabriel Bortoleto a 10-second time penalty.

As for Nico Hulkenberg, once he got rid of the inters, he spent the rest of the afternoon looking fast on the softs. So fast in fact that he was able to overtake two cars at once, before he managed to climb into the top 10 right at the end of the race. But he lost out to Lindblad on the very last lap, to finish just outside the points in P11 yet again.

Nico Hulkenberg, 11th

"It was an eventful race, and overall, we were in the fight for points but ultimately finished P11 again. I was much happier with my performance compared to yesterday. At the beginning we made the right call to switch to the intermediates early and, although it cost us initially, we recovered that within a lap. This put us in a good position for the rest of the race. "There was plenty of wheel-to-wheel racing. In the end, though, we just didn't quite have the pace to hold on to the points. Realistically, we only got into that position because of trouble to the cars ahead, so it was always going to be a long shot. Still, it was a clean race from my side, many learnings for us as a team and now it's straight on to Singapore.”

Gabriel Bortoleto, 18th

“First of all, I want to apologise to Carlos. I made contact with him at the restart and, unfortunately, compromised his race, as well as my own. I got damage to both my front wing and floor, and then we were too far behind to fight for anything. It wasn't a clean race after that either, it was a difficult Sunday overall. Now we take the positives and look ahead to Singapore: hopefully we can have a good result there.”

Allan McNish, Racing Director

“It was a difficult race. The weather conditions at the start were right on the edge, the crossover point between tyres, which was reflected by the split on the grid between slicks and intermediates. Already from the formation lap, it became clear to us that the intermediates were the correct choice, so we made the change and were able to recover to roughly the position we had been in before stopping for slicks on lap eight.

“Unfortunately, Gabi had contact with Sainz, which caused some damage and required an additional pit stop, and he ultimately received a ten-second penalty as well. That effectively took him out of the fight for points. Nico, on the other hand, had a strong run throughout the race: I think the strategy and the tyre choices we made were the right ones. Unfortunately, it wasn’t quite enough to bring us into the points, with Lindblad getting past Nico on the final lap.”

“It’s disappointing to miss out on the points on the final lap for the second race running. We have looked competitive throughout the weekend, but we need to keep working hard to manage to find a little more that will put us back in the top 10.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Alpine

Alpine’s day unravelled at a very early stage. They put both cars onto the softs, and Pierre Gasly had already spun off onto the wet grass before the standing start had even happened. Both fell backwards, and never managed to fully recover. The Frenchman stopped four times, as one of six drivers not to run the inters bar on those original two Formation Laps.

Franco Colapinto was another of those six, and while he only stopped three times, he spent most of the race on the unfavoured hard and medium compounds. On such a chaotic day, Alpine definitely missed out, while their biggest rival scored with both cars.

Pierre Gasly, 16th

“That was a tough day at the office. It was one of those days where it might go your way or it might not and, today, it clearly did not happen for us. After the suspended start, there was a long time waiting and we decided to start on Soft tyres. It made sense to all of us, and I supported the decision we made. I had a big moment on the formation lap trying to warm the tyres but managed to hang on and return to the track. It was a gamble which did not pay off as it was too wet and then took too long to dry and, like some others as well, we lost a lot of time on track. At that point you either have to come in and change the plan or try to make it work. We remained with our plan but, after that, everything seemed to go against us, there was nothing for us to capitalise on and, in the end, it was a painful day and a difficult result. We'll review everything as a team, stick together, and head to Singapore where we aim to return to the points. Finally, credit to the pit crew today. They had a busy afternoon with multiple stops and did a great job.”

Franco Colapinto, 13th

“It was a pity how the race played out today. Given my starting position on the grid, and having the added variable of rain, it meant I was in the right position to take that sort of risk with the tyres. I thought given the conditions at the start of the race, we could have taken advantage of them and made some big gains, but the track did not dry quick enough, and we lost a lot of time. It surprised me, and some others, that the track took so long to dry. With the high ambient temperatures and rough track surface, we thought the conditions would quickly come to us, but it did not happen in the end. It did not look wet and there was not much spray, but it was greasy with very little grip. In hindsight it was not the right decision, but after that we did the best we could to recover. The pace on the dry tyres was very good and hopefully bodes well for the future races, where we need to put in some strong and consistent performances as a team to try and reduce the gap in the standings, which is still doable with the number of races left.”

Flavio Briatore, Executive Advisor

“It was not the result we wanted today from where we started the race. Particularly with our competitors scoring and the current points difference in the Championship. We had performed well all weekend up until that point and looking at what happened in the race, we did not make the right calls or do a good enough job as a team. We, and some other teams, tried something different with the tyres and after that we did our best to recover but it did not pay off. However, the speed in the dry looked promising and there's still a lot of races left to chase down fifth place in the Championship.”

(Photo by Alex Bierens de Haan/LAT Images)

Haas

Not to be for Haas, with Esteban Ocon getting the closest to scoring in Malaysia. They split strategies at the start, sending Ollie Bearman out on softs and Ocon on inters. On a weekend where they have not had the same pace as their rivals, it was the right call, and favoured Ocon. The Frenchman was flirting with the top 10 for much of the race, but opted to stay out on his last set of softs after pitting just before the late VSC period, that became a Safety Car.

That cost Ocon, firstly in time lost, and secondly because his tyres lost more temperature behind the Safety Car due to being a few laps older. He also lost time running wide onto the grass on pit entry. The Frenchman fell down the order as a result when the race resumed, which was a shame after a strong afternoon.

Oliver Bearman, 14th

“I lost 40 seconds out there, so it was a long afternoon, but the car was really fast, I was flying and able to catch up, and I could see the points 10 seconds ahead of me. The positive thing is that if we had made the right choice at the start with tyres, we could’ve been fighting for points today. I hope that Singapore is a track that suits us more. I think the weather today helped us, being a bit cooler, but Singapore being a night race with a smooth track, those things should hopefully mean for a better weekend.”

Esteban Ocon, 15th

“We had an amazing start to the race, running in P6. Of course, we were not going to stay there, but we looked good for points. As soon as we made the stop, we started going backwards, so we need to look into a few things. It’s not the way we should end that race, and I’m sad for everyone who has done a good job on the car this weekend, but there are some choices we could’ve made differently. Potentially we could’ve kept fighting the Racing Bulls, where we should’ve been, but that’s not where we’ve finished.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“What an eventful race. Firstly, conditions were very tricky, so we decided to split the risk. I regret that decision – to not split the strategy, that was the right thing to do, but we really should’ve then boxed Ollie as soon as we realised how much lap time he was going to lose. We thought the track was going to dry a lot quicker, and that wasn’t the case. The positives are that Esteban’s pace on the first stint on inters was very strong, and also the first stint on soft tyres against Racing Bulls on hard were very strong. Unfortunately, on pit entry he went wide and our pit stop wasn’t the best, so we lost position to one of the Racing Bulls and then pushed the new tyres too hard, and from there, Esteban’s race got destroyed. It was a very challenging race, there were some positives – and areas where we were strong, but we need to take this as an opportunity to improve overall and focus for Singapore to get back into contention.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Charles Leclerc of Monaco driving the (16) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 and Esteban Ocon of France driving the (31) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari battle for track position at the race start during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain driving the (87) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Williams

On the intermediate tyres, both Williams cars climbed into the top 10 and looked on for a big haul of points. But while their afternoon might have started well, it certainly didn’t finish that way. Firstly, Alex Albon started to fall backwards after being double stacked, and then had to park up with a gearbox problem. It was the seventh time he has failed to see the chequered flag this season and second in a row.

Carlos Sainz’s quest for points was ended in a collision with Bortoleto, who punted the Spaniard into a spin. That dropped him down the field, and from there Sainz could not recover.

Carlos Sainz, 17th

“We did everything right at the start of the race and managed to climb all the way to P6. Unfortunately, after getting hit at the first restart I dropped quickly down the order and it was very tough for us to recover. It is a pity because we had a chance at holding on to a good result. We also need to look into race execution and make sure we have a better overall weekend next week in Singapore. We’ll try to bounce back and keep pushing."

Alex Albon, DNF

“A tricky race. We were on the right tyre at the start, the call for inters was spot on, and it was nice to be in the mix early on. Then the track dried out and we lost a bit of ground. The double stack didn't help, and with a flat spot on the softs we had to come in earlier than we wanted. We had a few issues throughout the race, including the brakes and a gearbox problem that ended our race. It's unfortunate, but we're lacking overall performance right now, and that's what we're really focusing on in our debriefs. We just want a smooth weekend and a feeling of progress, and we'll keep working to get that. I'm looking forward to Singapore, another home race for me, and hopefully we can fight further up the midfield."

James Vowles, Team Principal

“A difficult afternoon with moments where we looked to be in a good position, and, conversely, moments where we don't have the pace in order to be fighting for points at a track like this. It was an interesting day with rain coming in at exactly the right time causing a halt to proceedings whilst the monsoon passed. Then we had an unusual set of events where cars were unable to get around on their own power on the laps off the grid, requiring a red flag before we could start.

"It was a tricky call to determine whether to run the inters or slicks as everyone saw, so well done to the team for really committing with the inters; it was a good decision, and we were looking strong, as we pulled a clear pit stop gap, relative to cars behind. It was unfortunately short lived with a safety car that allowed everyone to close back in again, and from that point forwards, we didn't get it perfect, but also just simply didn't have the car pace we needed to make it work.

"We'll come back stronger in Singapore, but our focus is well and truly on getting this right for 2027."

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Carlos Sainz of Spain driving the (55) Williams FW48 Mercedes on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Alexander Albon of Thailand and Williams climbs out of his car after retiring from the race during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Cadillac

Valtteri Bottas was the first driver to head for an early shower, after the rear of his car stepped out on the soft tyres on the still wet track, the Finn spinning his Cadillac into the gravel trap. That brought out the first Safety Car, which proved influential on the fight up front.

As for Sergio Perez, he came through the pits an incredible seven times in the chaotic race. He swapped from the softs to the inters, back to the slicks and then just seemed to get unlucky with the timing of the Safety Cars.

Sergio Perez, 19th

“It was a very hard race today. We thought it was going to dry up a lot quicker than it did, but from the first lap I realised it was really difficult to keep the car on track.

“We made the decision to pit and, on the intermediates, the car was actually quite competitive and we were closing the gap to the cars ahead. We managed to put a great gap on the cars behind, so the strategy was looking good at that point.

“Unfortunately, the Safety Car came out and bunched the field back together, which took away the advantage we had built and changed the picture of the race. It was a very challenging race and the feeling in the car was difficult at times. Some cars had a software-related issue at the beginning, which affected the running, and I understand this is something the FIA is looking into closely. I’m sure we’ll learn from it and take those learnings forward into the future races.”

Valtteri Bottas, DNF

“It was always going to be a risk starting on the slicks with the soft tyre compound and today, it didn’t quite pay off. When the race started and I saw how fast the cars with the tntermediate tyres went through, you quickly realise the situation you’re in. We thought the track would dry quicker, and we thought it was worth trying something, but in the end it didn't work out. I took some risks trying to keep up with the pack and in the end it was my mistake that ended our race and I can only apologise to the team for that.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“Today was a challenging race and a new experience for the team with our first wet running of the season. We took the decision to start both cars on slicks after the red-flag restart, hoping the track would improve quickly, but the conditions ultimately made the intermediate tyres the better choice. Valtteri unfortunately lost the car at Turn 13 and had to retire early, while Checo brought the car to the finish and collected some valuable data for us. There is a lot for us to learn from today, particularly around tire behavior and car set-up in these conditions, and this experience will be important for the races ahead. We will regroup quickly and look forward to Singapore next weekend, which will present a different challenge.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Valtteri Bottas of Finland and Cadillac F1 Team sits on the back of a scooter of a marschal during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sona Maleterova/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 04: Sergio Perez of Mexico driving the (11) Cadillac F1 Team MAC-26 Ferrari on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 04, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

Pirelli

Dario Marrafuschi, Pirelli Motorsport Director

“Sepang provided the first real opportunity this season to see significant use of the Intermediate tyre. In the conditions encountered today, its performance was positive, delivering a high level of grip and consistent performance throughout its stint length. In the closing laps, as the track continued to dry, a slight amount of graining appeared on the wet-weather tyres, although there were no particular wear concerns despite the highly abrasive surface.

"The environmental conditions played a decisive role in the Malaysian Grand Prix. Temperatures were noticeably lower than those recorded in previous days and, following the downpour before the start, the track remained damp for much of the race. This helped keep tyre temperatures under control and reduced thermal degradation.

"In this scenario, the Soft proved particularly competitive, enabling very long stints and delivering consistent performance, helped by teams gradually bringing it into the operating window tested on Friday. Some drivers managed to cover almost half the race on the softest compound, while the neutralisations prompted many teams to opt for the C4 in the closing stages. Both the Hard and Medium also displayed consistent and predictable behaviour, albeit with lower grip levels than the Soft, confirming themselves as viable options for both the frontrunning teams and those in the midfield.”

title: Norris explains off-track moment behind Safety Car in Malaysia
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained what caused his dramatic run off track behind the Safety Car during the latter stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the incident dropping the Briton backwards en route to a final result of P9.

After the race start was initially delayed due to heavy rain – before a suspended start procedure followed – Norris was amongst those to bolt on the medium tyres for when the encounter eventually got underway. Those on slicks found themselves struggling in the mixed conditions, however, dropping the World Champion backwards from his original grid slot of P5.

An early Safety Car phase – following a stoppage for Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas – offered an opportunity to pit, which both Norris and team mate Oscar Piastri (who had swapped the medium tyres for intermediates at the end of the first lap) took advantage of.

There was further drama to come in the latter stages when, during another Safety Car period, Mercedes’ George Russell pulled to the side of the track on the main straight to retire his car, leading to those behind him bunching together.

This seemingly caught out Norris, who ran off track into the gravel after taking avoiding action around those ahead, dropping him back to P11. The British driver ultimately fought his way back to ninth when the race resumed, while Piastri ended the day in his original starting position of sixth.

Speaking to the media after the race, Norris conceded that the decision to start on the medium tyre had been “the wrong one”.

“There was enough of us that tried it, that obviously looked more convincing than it was, I guess, from the outside and from our laps to grid,” he explained.

“But I think the laps to grid and the inter tyre was a bit deceiving in terms of how much grip there was. I think a bit of it is also the fact we've never driven on the inter before and pushed on it, so it was hard for us to understand if it was like genuine, [if] the tyres were amazing or not.

“That also led to our decision, but in the end we got it wrong and I probably should have boxed at the end of the first lap, but we wanted to take the gamble.”

Norris went on to detail what led to his off-track excursion in the latter stages, with the 26-year-old subsequently summoned by the stewards for “driving erratically under Safety Car conditions, leaving the track and re-joining unsafely and/or overtaking another car behind the Safety Car”. In the end the Briton was issued with a reprimand.

“I swore a lot,” Norris admitted. “It's just I couldn't see from the angle and, from where I was, how much everyone had stopped because of George on the inside. So by the time I kind of looked at George and looked back, I could see them.

“But it's hard when you're directly behind to see if they're going 100, 200, or 10, and they were going 10, so I just got completely caught out. I guess it's my fault at the end of the day, so I was just unlucky with it. Everyone just checked up so much and I just got screwed over by it, that's all.”

title: 'P2 was the maximum we could have achieved' – Antonelli
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli sits 84 points clear at the top of the Drivers' Championship following his P2 finish at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – with team mate and rival George Russell retiring towards the end – but insists the Mercedes team “still have work to do”.

The Italian started from third on the grid in Sunday's race in Sepang, and chose intermediate tyres for the mixed conditions at lights out – which proved to be the right choice as he overtook polesitter Max Verstappen on the run down to Turn 1.

Antonelli then lost ground to the Dutch driver after the first Safety Car, brought out by Valtteri Bottas beaching his car in the gravel, but managed to see off a challenge by Russell to stay second.

Running in P2, he was already set to extend his lead in the championship by three points when his team mate had his race cut short on Lap 50 with a suspected power unit failure behind another Safety Car – dealing a blow to the Briton’s already slim title chances.

The 20-year-old said afterwards that Mercedes still had “a lot of work to do” as the team had been “struggling”, but added he was satisfied with finishing second to Verstappen.

"I think today was the maximum we could have done," he explained. "Massive congrats to Max and Red Bull for the incredible weekend. And on our side, a lot of work to do – we've been struggling a bit more than usual, but still really happy to come away with P2."

Speaking to the media post-race, Antonelli added: "I’m really happy with P2. It’s a result we deserved because we’ve been... Well, to be fair, after the start I thought we could have had a chance to win today.

"But then after the restart, you know, Max overtook me, also George overtook me. Then I was able to regain P2, and then from that point on I was there in P2 the whole time. So yeah, that was what we deserved today."

When asked about Russell's DNF, Antonelli said it was a disappointing result for his team mate and Mercedes overall.

“It’s obviously a big shame for him and the team as well, because it would have been a good result for the team," he said. "But unfortunately we’ve been suffering from this reliability this year. I’m sure the team is doing its best to understand where the issue is coming from and make sure it doesn’t happen again.”

It was Russell’s second mechanical DNF of the season after also failing to finish in Canada, whilst Antonelli had to retire from the Grand Prix in Barcelona with a power unit problem.

Despite his lead at the top of the drivers' standings, Antonelli says he’s taking nothing for granted, and the issues they’ve had with reliability impacts the way he goes into each race weekend.

“[Reliability is] why it’s really important that whenever I go on track, especially with things in my control, I need to make sure that I do my best,” he added.

title: Hamilton reflects on 'bittersweet' comeback podium in Malaysia
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton says his podium finish at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was “bittersweet” after completing a comeback drive to P3 having at one stage been a minute behind the leaders.

The race in Sepang was initially delayed due to thunderstorms in the area, and the first race start procedure then got suspended as several drivers, including Hamilton, struggled to maintain speed on the initial formation lap.

When the race eventually got under way in mixed conditions, the Briton – who was second on the grid after a strong performance in Qualifying – dropped 15 places having opted to fit his Ferrari with slick soft tyres instead of intermediates.

With the track not drying up as quickly as hoped, Hamilton dropped to P17 to run a minute behind the leading cars on the first lap – prompting the Scuderia to suggest a switch.

However, the seven-time World Champion made the call from the cockpit to "gamble" and stay on the softs instead – a decision that ultimately saw him roar through the field to cross the line third behind Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli.

Asked how he felt after the race, Hamilton wasn’t sure. “I think it’s bittersweet," he said. "We had an opportunity and ultimately didn’t maximise it.

"I had a tough [time] at the beginning, but after the race got going and I managed to keep it on track — which, I’m telling you, was so, so hard.

“I didn’t think that I’d be able to get back to third place, so I’m very, very grateful for that and very happy with it.”

"Obviously we had the wrong call in the beginning, which was so difficult and I could see everyone just pulling away," he added. "I could see on the screen it was a minute down, and I thought that was kind of race over for us. But I just kept my head down, the guys did a great job with the pit stops – obviously lots of tyre changes and lots of chasing."

Although Hamilton felt like it was a missed opportunity, he is looking more comfortable in his Ferrari than in recent races.

He told media it was one of his better weekends in red: “I think we did a really good job yesterday. The engineers did a great job, the mechanics did a great job with changing and fixing the car, getting the car where it needed to be.

excerpt:

In a race Max Verstappen won the first grand prix for Red Bull's in-house power unit, the French driver could only finish in fifth, despite looking set for a podium finish.

After clearing Liam Lawson early on, Hadjar cemented his position in fourth, behind Verstappen and the two Mercedes drivers, but after the retirement of George Russell, Hadjar was promoted to run third behind the safety car.

"I had no pace; something was wrong. I was maybe losing a second a lap compared to the Mercedes," Hadjar told media, including RacingNews365.

"The whole weekend we were quicker, and in the race, we were absolutely nowhere. The car was horrible to drive, and in the last couple of laps, I don't know how we ended up with no battery on the straight, so I couldn't defend against the Ferraris.

"Otherwise, I would have kept third, but I just had no grip. Even behind the safety car, I was feeling that I had no grip, and it was going to be a tough restart as it felt I was always on the same tyre.

"It's not a good day for me; I'm happy for the team, but it is a disaster."

title: Max Verstappen sets new F1 record under bizarre circumstances
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's victory in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia set a new all-time F1 record for the longest gap between wins at the same circuit.

From pole, Verstappen recorded a hat-trick on his way to the first-ever victory for Red Bull-Ford Powertrains - a historic moment for the team with its in-house unit.

The victory, the 72nd of Verstappen's career, came at Sepang after it stepped in to host the Bahrain GP, which was unable to do so at Sakhir due to the Iran War and was postponed from its April date.

Sepang offered to step in, marking F1's return to Malaysia for the first time since 2017, when the government decided to stop cancel the race owing to falling attendance.

That final Malaysian GP was won by Verstappen for his second grand prix victory, and nine years later, he claimed victory at Sepang once again.

This nine-year and three day gap translates into 3,291 days, and shatters the previous record of Nigel Mansell.

The win, which will officially count as a Bahrain GP victory, is Verstappen's third in that particular race, after his 2023 and 2024 successes.

Mansell won the 1985 South African Grand Prix at Kyalami in the final race in the country under the Apartheid regime, with then FIA president Jean-Marie Balestre declaring that F1 would not race again in the country until Apartheid was over.

Nelson Mandela was released from prison on Robben Island in February 1990, with sporting events returning to South Africa over the next few years, including the F1 grand prix at Kyalami in 1992.

Mansell would go on to win this first race back in 1992, 2,325 days after the 1985 race.

The South African Grand Prix would run for two years upon its return in the early 1990s, with the 1993 race being won by Alain Prost - the final time to date F1 has raced in Africa, with repeated attempts to return to the continent, including at Kyalami and in Rwanda emerging in the last few years.

title: WRC crowns champion after rival crashes on penultimate corner whilst set to take title
excerpt:
Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin have been crowned 2026 World Rally Championship champions after title rival Oliver Solberg crashed just two corners from the finish of the final powerstage of the Rally Italia Sardegna, handing Evans the crown in the most dramatic possible fashion.

Evans becomes the first British world champion in 25 years, and only the third Briton ever to win the title, following in the footsteps of the late Richard Burns, who lifted the crown in 2001, and the late Colin McRae.

Going into the powerstage in Sardinia, the title picture was on a knife edge. Solberg — whose father, Petter, won the WRC title in 2003 — led the rally outright while Evans sat fifth, and the Swede also topped the Super Sunday standings, with Evans set to score nothing after stopping to change a puncture on the penultimate stage.

It meant the two title protagonists — and Toyota Gazoo Racing WRT team-mates — were effectively separated by a single point, with the powerstage result set to decide the championship.

Evans had all but given up hope after completing his own powerstage run, admitting he had "overdriven" the Sassari test.

Alarm bells rang further when Sami Pajari, running two cars behind Evans, went 2.2 seconds quicker, a sign that running higher up the road through the rutted, sandy stage was far from an advantage.

Solberg then set about erasing the deficit. He was fastest of all at the first split and, though he couldn't live with Thierry Neuville's pace, was 1.9 seconds up on Evans with just 1.2 kilometres left to run.

Solberg two corners from glory

But the title bid unravelled in an instant. With only two corners remaining, Solberg lost the rear on a left-hander, snapped the car the other way and speared off the road.

Solberg recovered to complete the stage and still won the rally outright, beating Sébastien Ogier by 57.6 seconds.

But the crash cost him nine seconds on the powerstage compared to Evans, enough to hand the championship to the Welshman.

"I don't think it's quite sunk in yet," said Evans. "I was quite sure that was over. I didn't drive the best stage; I threw everything at it, but it wasn't clean.

"I feel for Oliver as well; he did an incredible weekend. I'm sorry for him to lose it so close to the finish. But we have a lot of people to thank for backing me over the years, Scotty [Martin] for an incredible job."

Solberg was left inconsolable at the finish, having come within a few hundred metres of becoming world champion before crashing in sight of the line.

Team principal Jari-Matti Latvala and Ogier had to coax him onto the powerstage podium, where he struggled to hold back emotion as the Swedish national anthem played despite falling short of the title.

title: Fernando Alonso slates '100%' unfair decision after Lewis Hamilton reprieve

After being given a reset, Hamilton got the Ferrari moving again, but was nearly 'lapped' by pole-sitter Max Verstappen, who himself had overcome a gremlin, with the FIA then quickly suspending the start sequence due to the chaos, and red-flagging the event.

Under the delay whilst the software bug was fixed, the decision was taken to have the cars put back in original grid order for the standing start, meaning Hamilton took up his second place.

After falling to the rear on his slick tyres at this start, Hamilton rallied and banked an unlikely podium in third, with Alonso also taking Aston Martin's best result of the season in eighth place - more than doubling the team's points haul from three to seven in one swoop.

Reflecting, the two-time champion was surprised at the decision for the race to be put back in grid order.

When then asked for his thoughts on cars stopping behind the safety car, Alonso said: "The same thing that goes through [the FIA's] mind when they see the Aston Martin stop and sit on one side because they have a problem and good because you have one less car in the race."

Alonso then claimed it was "100% unfair that the grid order was reset to the original starting positions once the grand prix finally did get underway, over 90 minutes late.

"100%," he answered directly if the decision was unfair.

"I mean, this is motor racing. If it is a safety concern, I get it. If there are five cars in the middle of the road, we have to stop the race and see what is going on.

"But I think [the cars that stopped] were out of the race. They were at the wall, and the marshals just had to push it two metres and retire the car, like we do at 50% of the races.

"It is the first time I see it, but right now, I don't have all the information, so there is no clear explanation, and it is okay, and I'm not too concerned.

"From our side, we try to do our job, try to keep the car running, and then the rain was very much appreciated in terms of opportunities for us."
