title: Lando Norris learns stewards' verdict after Bahrain GP investigation
excerpt:
While following the Safety Car, NOR approached Turn 1 behind a group of cars. Car 63 (George Russell) had stopped with a mechanical problem ahead of Turn 1, which caused the cars ahead of NOR to slow down. NOR explained that, due to the low sun and resulting visibility conditions, it was difficult to recognise that the cars ahead had started to slow earlier than would normally have been expected.

NOR consequently misjudged his closing speed and approached the cars ahead too quickly. When he realised this, he braked heavily and deliberately steered to the left, onto the kerbs and then into the gravel bed in order to avoid contact with the cars ahead. By driving onto the kerbs, NOR had reduced grip available for braking, which further limited his ability to slow the car.

In doing so, NOR momentarily overshot Car 81 (Oscar Piastri), who was directly ahead of him. The Stewards considered whether this constituted an overtake while the Safety Car was deployed. Although NOR momentarily moved ahead of PIA, this occurred solely as a consequence of NOR leaving the track while taking avoiding action.

PIA immediately repassed NOR while NOR was off the track. The Stewards therefore determined that this did not constitute an overtaking manoeuvre and take no further action in respect of this aspect of the incident. The Stewards also considered that, particularly while driving behind the Safety Car, NOR should have managed the gap to the cars ahead and his closing speed with greater care.

The prevailing visibility conditions were circumstances which NOR should have taken into account when determining an appropriate speed and gap to he cars ahead, rather than a reason which excused the resulting driving. The need for heavy braking and an avoiding manoeuvre into the gravel demonstrated that NOR had not maintained an appropriate margin in the circumstances.

The Stewards therefore determined that NOR had driven erratically in breach of Article B5.13.2a of the FIA F1 Regulations. Such a situation should not arise while driving behind the Safety Car, and NOR was required to maintain a sufficient margin to the cars ahead. However, taking into account that NOR reacted promptly once he recognised the situation and successfully avoided contact, the Stewards consider a Reprimand as appropriate.

The Stewards separately considered NOR's return to the track. Although Car 18 (Lance Stroll) was in relative close proximity, NOR returned progressively and without requiring STR to take avoiding action or otherwise creating an unsafe situation. The Stewards therefore determined that the re-join was safe.

The Stewards also reviewed whether, after having re-joined the track, NOR had overtaken STR while the Safety Car was deployed. The video evidence showed that, as NOR returned from the gravel, he had already crossed the white line with at least one wheel and, as such, was back on track. At this point, he was ahead of STR and at no point did NOR pass STR. Rather, STR approached NOR while NOR was already in the process of returning to the track. The Stewards therefore determined that NOR had not overtaken STR under Safety Car conditions and as such also take no further action for this part of the incident.

title: Audi receive huge F1 fine after Nico Hulkenberg statement released
excerpt:
Audi has been handed a €30,000 fine by F1 stewards, €20,000 of which is suspended for an unsafe situation involving Nico Hulkenberg and a mechanic in the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

At the final stop under the late safety car, there was confusion after Hulkenberg appeared to move off whilst the front wing flap angle was being adjusted by a mechanic.

The German had received a green light, indicating to him to pull away, but he stopped within 0.2s and avoided contact with the mechanic, as part of the team's release procedure, where an additional manual safety check is carried out by a controller.

This controller stopped the car by turning the light back to red, thus stopping Hulkenberg, whose car was found to have not passed by the point under which an unsafe releasre would have been declared.

The stewards felt that whilst no unsafe release had occured, an unsafe situation had been caused by the early release and handed Audi the €30,000 fine, two-thirds of which is suspended for one year.

It means that provided Audi is not involved in a similar offence in the next 12 months, it will only pay €10,000.

Hulkenberg would ultimately go onto finish in 11th place for the fourth time this season, narrowly being pipped to a point by Arvid Lindblad's Racing Bulls machine.

"In response to queries regarding Nico's pit-stop during today's race, we can confirm that there was no contact made between the car and the crew member on the front left of the car," began an Audi statement, issued to media, including RacingNews365.

"While the front wing adjuster remained stuck, the system reacted, and after 0.2s of green light, the red light was shown again to signal the driver to stop.

"Nico reacted to this, and the operator finished the operation safely. The crew member was unaffected and took part in all the team's subsequent pit stops."

The article continues below.

Hulkenberg's reflections

After his 11th place, Hulkenberg wished his best to the mechanic involved.

"The guy who does the front wing, somehow his screwdriver got stuck," Hulkenberg told media, including RacingNews365.

"It wasn't the cleanest stop, but I hope he is okay."

Turning to the formation lap chaos, Hulkenberg described the events as "peculiar."

"It was very peculiar and strange, and it was a hell of a day with so many weird things happening in the race, so there's a lot to take in and digest."

title: FIA vow to launch 'full review' into Bahrain GP formation lap carnage
excerpt:
The FIA has vowed to launch a "full review" into the carnage seen on the formation laps at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

With the start of the grand prix delayed by 40 minutes due to rain, the field eventually pulled away for two formation laps to sight the track conditions, but a number of cars either slowed to a crawl or stopped completely.

Pole-sitter Max Verstappen was one of these, with second-placed Lewis Hamilton falling down the order as his machine stopped on the back-straight after holding the field up. Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas also stopped before the start sequence was suspended and red flags flown.

This suspension lasted for just under one hour, with a software patch being worked on and immediately transferred to the teams as a fix, with the race then resuming without any further similar trouble.

The formation laps were the first time the 2026-spec F1 cars have tried a formation lap in competition in wet conditions, with the only previous wet weather running coming in Pirelli tyre testing or in pre-season shakedowns.

FIA single-seater technical director Nikolas Tombazis explained that the confusion was essentially down to the software "not being tested in those specific conditions" as he explained how the FIA had quickly implemented a fix.

The governing body then issued a formal statement, confirming that the issue "had not been detected by the FIA or teams" until it was too late.

The full statement is available below.

FIA statement in full

On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars.

As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the Power Unit before the start of the race.

This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and Power Unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue."

title: Lewis Hamilton explains 'Lego race' replay farce before 'big panic' set in
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has described the initial formation lap of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia as akin to "the Lego race" before "big panic" set in as he lost all power to his Ferrari.

Following a thunderstorm and torrential downpour at the Sepang International Circuit that sparked a 40-minute delay, the drivers finally set off behind the safety car, only to encounter almost immediate issues.

FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis has confirmed that "a bug" caused software problems, compounded by the fact the cars were running at slow speeds given the conditions.

At the head of the field after clinching pole position, Max Verstappen almost stopped on track. That sparked a concertina effect through the field, forcing others to drive slowly as the bug prevented the power from being redeployed.

Eventually, Hamilton, who was due to start second, ground to a halt on the start-finish straight. Another lengthy delay followed as the FIA was forced to update the software.

Verstappen and Hamilton, who went on to finish first and third at the chequered flag that fell three hours and 20 minutes after the race was initially due to start, were able to look back and laugh at what unfolded.

Asked about the complicated nature of the engines, and for F1 to end up in the situation it did, Verstappen said: "That's the problem that we have.

"These engines are so complicated, and a lot of software is implemented, and when there is something like this, that's the problem.

"I triggered it first, and then I looked in my mirror; I just saw...and I was like, 'Wait. Are they waiting for me? What's going on?"

[Article continues below]

Antonelli - 'It was insane'

Hamilton quickly chipped in, stating: "It was like the Lego race! We had the same speed!"

That was a reference to the drivers racing in Lego F1 cars ahead of the 2025 Miami GP and in Lego go-karts prior to this year's British GP.

Mercedes driver and championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who finished second, added: "It was insane. At some point, we were five wide in the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on."

Verstappen then took up the story. "Then we did a lap, and then I saw eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you [turning to Hamilton] by yourself crawling."

Hamilton added: "Well, I had to stop on track, stop the engine and restart it. I've never done that before."

Verstappen then concluded: "What can you say? I mean, that's not what you want for the sport? Hopefully, there is a lesson learned."

title: Christian Horner takes to social media after 'incredible' Red Bull F1 achievement
excerpt:
Former Red Bull Christian Horner has taken to social media to offer his congratulations after the team took its first F1 victory with its own engine in the Bahrain GP.

Max Verstappen emerged victorious from the chaotic grand prix, to record Red Bull's first victory of the season - and crucially, the first since it switched to its own Red Bull-Ford Powertrain.

The decision was taken under Horner's tenure to take the step to become a power unit manufacturer for 2026, with the factory beginning to be built up under him, with the likes of Ben Hodgkinson signed to lead the project.

Since leaving Red Bull in July 2025, Horner has seldom commented on Red Bull, but took to Instagram stories, below, to offer his congratulations.

RBPT-Ford is just the 23rd different engine manufacturer to win a grand prix in F1.

title: FIA issue apology after on-track stoppages cause Bahrain GP chaos
excerpt:
FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis has issued an apology to F1 fans after a startling series of on-track stoppages caused a delay to the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Following a postponement due to adverse weather conditions, the cars finally emerged from the pit lane behind the safety car in wet conditions some 40 minutes after the scheduled race start.

However, as they rounded the track, some cars began to slow down, with Max Verstappen at the head of the field highlighting that he felt as though he had no power.

Three cars were spotted stopping on the racetrack - Lewis Hamilton, Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas - before they fired back up and got going again.

With the field running at such a slow pace behind Verstappen, who streaked into the distance, the four-time champion amazingly came around to lap the field, with the safety car now running behind some cars.

It caused the FIA to abort the start and, after all of the cars returned to the pit lane, the power units were diagnosed with a bug, which required a software update to fix.

Explaining the situation, Tombazis said: "There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars and some cars almost stopped completely.

"That bug prevented the power from being redeployed and for the cars to start again.

"If we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not to have such a situation.

"Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software, which was issued to the teams, and the teams had to install it on their cars.

"So all of that took about 20 minutes. It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting for a race and for everybody else, which is understandable.

"We are sorry about that, but I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem."

[Article continues below]

Tombazis: Software not tested in such slow conditions

The opening stages of the race around the Sepang International Circuit marked the first time this year the cars had run extensively in wet conditions.

With the wet surface under a formation lap naturally causing a lower-than-normal speed, the power units were effectively unable to keep firing.

Tombazis has acknowledged that the FIA missed putting the software through such tests at low speed when preparing it for its debut as part of the new cycle of regulations.

"The software was tested, it just wasn't tested in those specific conditions," Tombazis said.

"What caught us out was the fact that cars went at that very, very low speed, which was not normally contemplated.

"When problems happen, people learn. Everything you do, from the phone you're holding, everything is based on learning things and improving.

"I'm not saying that no error happened, the bug is, by definition, an error.

"Testing stuff better avoids errors. That's obviously what people try to do.

"Sometimes things fall through the net, and people learn, and you do a better job next time."

title: George Russell 'beyond disappointment' after F1 title blow: 'You've got to laugh'
excerpt:
George Russell has said "you've almost got to laugh" at his bad luck after retiring from a near-certain third in the closing stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Russell was behind Kimi Antonelli during the late safety car period when a suspected power unit issue meant he had to pull over to one side, turning a net three-point loss into an 18-point loss in the F1 drivers' title fight.

It leaves the British driver 84 points adrift of his Mercedes team-mate in the championship standings with just six or seven rounds of the campaign to go.

"You've almost got to laugh," Russell told Sky Sports F1 after the race. "I'm beyond disappointment. So many times this season it's happened; it's a real shame... but just keep on fighting, just keep on trying to go.

"The podium, of course, looked very certain. Solid race, not an amazing race, but a solid race.

"But not the first time, so I'm pretty used to this feeling and these questions, let's say."

Russell: 'I needed luck on my side'

Having started seventh, the early chaos saw Russell vault his way up to third, before getting the better of Antonelli at the first safety car restart.

However, he could not hold onto the young Italian, who was extracting better pace from his W17, and looked to have secured a three-point loss in the standings. Not ideal, but perhaps more than he could have expected before the race.

But for fate to intervene in his season again, as it did so often during the opening rounds of the year, meaning any hope of an improbable recovery in the F1 drivers' title fight now looks to be beyond reach.

"I don't need to say, 'I think it's gone' or whatever, but of course it's exceptionally likely, and that's just the reality," Russell replied when asked if he must now accept the championship is over.

"I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I've had luck not on my side, so you know, a three-point loss today, being behind Kimi, turned into an 18-point loss.

"Of course, if the issue was on the other side, it would have been an 18-point gain. So it's a real shame... but that's just how it is."
